power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .196", "p = .13"), Sentence = c("Trust in perception increased by 2.4 points, with a confidence interval spanning zero [-1.0, 5.9] and Holm-adjusted p = .196.", "The image-level rank association was positive but imprecise with only six stimuli (reported ρ = .70, p = .13)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Declaration of generative AI in the writing process: During the preparation of this work, the authors used generative AI tools (Claude, Anthropic; ChatGPT, OpenAI) to assist with language editing, restructuring and drafting of manuscript text, formatting of references, and preparation of data figures from author-computed summary statistics.
These tools were not used for study design, data collection, or statistical analysis, which were conducted solely by the authors.
After using these tools, the authors reviewed, verified, and edited all content, and take full responsibility for the content of the manuscript.
A visitor may leave an exhibition feeling calmer, puzzled by an illusion, or newly attentive to the way a first impression forms.
These responses matter to cultural leisure, but they are not interchangeable.

Feeling relaxed does not demonstrate recovered attentional capacity; reporting a new idea does not establish enduring learning; and participating alongside others does not necessarily produce belonging.

Leisure research offers resources for understanding this complexity, from accounts of experiences unfolding over time to analyses of meaning, embodiment, and the social conditions of participation (Stewart, 1998; Iwasaki, 2008; Packer & Ballantyne, 2016).
text.formatted: Leisure research offers resources for understanding this complexity, from accounts of experiences unfolding over time to analyses of meaning, embodiment, and the social conditions of participation <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Stewart, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Iwasaki, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Packer & Ballantyne, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The challenge for an exhibition evaluation is therefore not simply to establish that visitors enjoyed themselves.
It is to specify which aspects of experience were supported, what evidence bears on those aspects, and what another provider could reasonably do with the findings.
Research already connects leisure engagement with subjective well-being and identifies multiple possible pathways between participation and health (Kuykendall et al., 2015; Fancourt et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Research already connects leisure engagement with subjective well-being and identifies multiple possible pathways between participation and health <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Kuykendall et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Fancourt et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Educational leisure scholarship also demonstrates that enjoyment and discovery need not be competing purposes (Packer, 2006), while museum research identifies possibilities for restoration in cultural as well as natural environments (Packer & Bond, 2010).
text.formatted: Educational leisure scholarship also demonstrates that enjoyment and discovery need not be competing purposes <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Packer, 2006)</ref>, while museum research identifies possibilities for restoration in cultural as well as natural environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Packer & Bond, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: A further demonstration that a short cultural visit can be enjoyable or beneficial would, by itself, add little to these established arguments.

A more useful contribution is to examine how particular arrangements of cultural leisure bring bodily experience, explanation, and reflection into relation, while distinguishing the experience a setting invites from the outcome an evaluation actually measures.
Art of Perception provides a case through which to examine that distinction.

The free exhibition, presented within Creative Lab Festival 2026 in Pune, India, combined seven zones addressing breathing and heartbeat, movement, aesthetic interpretation, visual illusions, social judgment, neurodivergent artistic expression, and the surrounding botanical garden.

Several installations made visitors' own sensing and judging part of the content: movement generated imagery, breathing was accompanied by physiological feedback, and individual judgments contributed to a visible distribution of votes.
Rather than only communicating information about perception, the exhibition invited visitors to notice themselves perceiving.
We use embodied reflexivity to describe this design invitation: attending to how one senses, interprets, or judges while participating in an activity.
The term identifies a relationship between experience and reflection, not a measured psychological trait or a claim that visitors necessarily became more self-aware.
It brings the case into conversation with leisure scholarship in which bodily activity is a way of knowing, rather than merely the delivery mechanism for a cognitive message (Borovica, 2020).
text.formatted: It brings the case into conversation with leisure scholarship in which bodily activity is a way of knowing, rather than merely the delivery mechanism for a cognitive message <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Borovica, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: It also makes the evaluation question more specific: what happens when cultural leisure invites people both to undergo an experience and to consider how that experience is being made?
This paper offers three connected contributions.

Empirically, it describes a differentiated profile of immediate self-reported responses in an arts-science exhibition outside the predominantly Anglophone institutional settings represented by much of the literature discussed here.
Conceptually, it connects embodied learning with restorative and reflective possibilities without treating them as identical outcomes.

Methodologically and practically, it develops a designexperience-evidence matrix: an explicit separation of opportunities provided, responses documented, and explanations or longer-term benefits still to be tested.
This is an interpretive tool derived from the case, not a validated causal model.
The analysis addresses three questions.
What immediate changes were recorded in visitors' selfreported bodily state, beliefs about perception and first impressions, and connection to nature?
What additional aspects of participation appear in written responses, installation votes, and workshop drawings, and where do these materials fail to corroborate the survey?
Finally, how can those findings inform cultural leisure design and evaluation without assuming that free admission ensures inclusion or that participation establishes a health benefit?
The argument concerns the organization and interpretation of situated leisure experiences, rather than a contrast between serious and casual leisure.
Experience-centered leisure research directs attention away from an activity label alone and toward what happens before, during, and after participation.

Stewart's (1998) multiphase account challenges the treatment of leisure as a single, stable event. Packer and Ballantyne's (2016) multifaceted model likewise recognizes that visitor experience encompasses several dimensions rather than a uniform response to a venue.
text.formatted: Stewart's (1998) multiphase account challenges the treatment of leisure as a single, stable event. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Packer and Ballantyne's (2016)</ref> multifaceted model likewise recognizes that visitor experience encompasses several dimensions rather than a uniform response to a venue.

text.text: These approaches make room for different experiences within the same visit and for differences between the experience anticipated, experienced, and subsequently remembered. Duerden et al. (2018) distinguish memorable, meaningful, and transformational experiences through their relationships with emotion, discovery, and change.
text.formatted: These approaches make room for different experiences within the same visit and for differences between the experience anticipated, experienced, and subsequently remembered. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Duerden et al. (2018)</ref> distinguish memorable, meaningful, and transformational experiences through their relationships with emotion, discovery, and change.

text.text: The importance of this distinction here is evidential: an immediately salient encounter need not reorganize a visitor's life or retain its significance after departure.
An exit survey can capture a present appraisal, but claims about transformation require evidence beyond that appraisal.
The relevant question is therefore not whether an exhibition qualifies as an extraordinary experience for everyone, but which dimensions of an encounter are documented and on what timescale.
This perspective also limits what design can claim.
We use affordance in the modest sense of an opportunity for action or experience that becomes available in a particular setting.
An opportunity to sit quietly is not the same as feeling free to do so; a prompt for reflection may be welcomed, ignored, or experienced as instruction.
Drawing together experience-centered and contextual accounts, we treat design as arranging possibilities that visitors encounter through
The DRAMMA framework identifies five proposed psychological domains linking leisure and subjective well-being: detachment-recovery, autonomy, mastery, meaning, and affiliation (Newman et al., 2014).
text.formatted: The DRAMMA framework identifies five proposed psychological domains linking leisure and subjective well-being: detachment-recovery, autonomy, mastery, meaning, and affiliation <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Newman et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: It is useful for generating questions about experiences that might matter, but a setting designed with those possibilities in mind has not thereby demonstrated them.

In the present study, bodily relaxation is relevant to recovery, yet does not measure detachment from demands; reporting an idea about perception is not equivalent to mastery; and access to a selfpaced route does not establish experienced autonomy.
We use the framework as an interpretive reference, not as a measurement model tested by the six survey items.

A complementary multilevel account locates potential leisure-health pathways in psychological, biological, social, and behavioral processes operating beyond the individual alone (Fancourt et al., 2021).
text.formatted: A complementary multilevel account locates potential leisure-health pathways in psychological, biological, social, and behavioral processes operating beyond the individual alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Fancourt et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This matters because explanations centered exclusively on the visitor's brain can obscure the relationships and conditions through which participation becomes possible.
The exhibition's scientific content is part of its design, not a reason to reduce leisure experience to a neural or physiological event.

Leisure scholarship on embodiment offers a more expansive starting point. Borovica's (2020) creative inquiry uses dance to explore bodily knowing in relation to objects and the meanings of womanhood. Fullagar (2008), examining women's experiences of recovery from depression, attends to emotion-work and emotion-play rather than construing leisure as a standardized corrective to an individual deficit.
text.formatted: Leisure scholarship on embodiment offers a more expansive starting point. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Borovica's (2020)</ref> creative inquiry uses dance to explore bodily knowing in relation to objects and the meanings of womanhood. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Fullagar (2008)</ref>, examining women's experiences of recovery from depression, attends to emotion-work and emotion-play rather than construing leisure as a standardized corrective to an individual deficit.

text.text: More recently, Borovica et al. (2026) show how creative and leisure practices can support self-discovery while remaining entangled with the difficulties and politics of living with mental distress.
text.formatted: More recently, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Borovica et al. (2026)</ref> show how creative and leisure practices can support self-discovery while remaining entangled with the difficulties and politics of living with mental distress.

text.text: These studies involve different populations and methods from the present evaluation.
Their relevance is conceptual: embodied experience is situated, relational, and not uniformly positive.

An arts-science encounter may consequently invite reflection without necessarily improving well-being, and may be valuable without resembling treatment. Fancourt et al. (2026) discuss common processes across arts-based leisure and psychological therapies in a conceptual Personal View.
text.formatted: An arts-science encounter may consequently invite reflection without necessarily improving well-being, and may be valuable without resembling treatment. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Fancourt et al. (2026)</ref> discuss common processes across arts-based leisure and psychological therapies in a conceptual Personal View.

text.text: That comparison does not erase differences in intention, professional context, or therapeutic relationships.

It provides a reason to investigate mechanisms carefully, not to label a public exhibition therapeutic on the basis of immediate self-report. Iwasaki's (2008) work on meaning-making in global contexts connects leisure-like pursuits with identity, cultural and social relationships, learning, and ways of responding to life's difficulties.
text.formatted: It provides a reason to investigate mechanisms carefully, not to label a public exhibition therapeutic on the basis of immediate self-report. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Iwasaki's (2008)</ref> work on meaning-making in global contexts connects leisure-like pursuits with identity, cultural and social relationships, learning, and ways of responding to life's difficulties.

text.text: This approach discourages treating meaning as an individual score detached from everyday circumstances.

In a garden-based exhibition, connection to nature may likewise involve more than temporary relaxation. Vuong and Nguyen's (2024) conceptual discussion of the kingfisher considers how artistic, scientific, and remembered encounters can mediate human-nature relationships.
text.formatted: In a garden-based exhibition, connection to nature may likewise involve more than temporary relaxation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Vuong and Nguyen's (2024)</ref> conceptual discussion of the kingfisher considers how artistic, scientific, and remembered encounters can mediate human-nature relationships.

text.text: Such accounts broaden the questions worth asking; they do not demonstrate ecological commitment or behavioral change in the present visitors.
Access also extends beyond an admission price.
The leisure-constraints literature distinguishes intrapersonal, interpersonal, and structural constraints on participation (Crawford et al., 1991).
text.formatted: The leisure-constraints literature distinguishes intrapersonal, interpersonal, and structural constraints on participation <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Crawford et al., 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Removing a fee addresses one potential barrier, while questions remain about transport, time, language, care responsibilities, physical access, and whether the setting feels welcoming.
We therefore treat free admission as a documented feature of provision, not a demonstrated equity outcome.
Attendance data describe those recorded at the venue, not those who could not attend or chose not to do so.

Inclusion must also concern whose creativity and expertise are recognized. Darcy et al. (2022) foreground artistic impact and career development in disability arts, extending attention beyond benefits experienced by audiences.
text.formatted: Inclusion must also concern whose creativity and expertise are recognized. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Darcy et al. (2022)</ref> foreground artistic impact and career development in disability arts, extending attention beyond benefits experienced by audiences.

text.text: Their argument is pertinent to an exhibition displaying work by neurodivergent artists: those artists should not be reduced to instruments for producing visitors' empathy or well-being.

In another context, MacRitchie et al.'s (2023) review of technology-supported arts activities with people living with cognitive impairment or dementia highlights the relevance of choice, personalization, and co-design.
These are useful considerations for future provision here, not evidence that this exhibition was accessible to those populations or co-designed with them.

Creative methods can reveal aspects of leisure that standardized response options fail to express. Parry and Johnson (2007) argue for creative analytic practices capable of representing complexity in lived leisure experience. Schultz and Legg (2020) introduce a/r/tography as an arts-based methodology in which artistic, research, and teaching practices are interconnected.
text.formatted: Creative methods can reveal aspects of leisure that standardized response options fail to express. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Parry and Johnson (2007)</ref> argue for creative analytic practices capable of representing complexity in lived leisure experience. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Schultz and Legg (2020)</ref> introduce a/r/tography as an arts-based methodology in which artistic, research, and teaching practices are interconnected.

text.text: Both challenge the assumption that an artwork is useful to research only once its features have been converted into categories.
Their relevance to this evaluation is also cautionary: soliciting and counting drawings does not, by itself, constitute a/r/tographic inquiry or an interpretive account of participants' lives.
There is a further distinction between participation in an activity and participation in governing research.

Contributing a token or a written response need not entail involvement in deciding the questions, interpreting the material, or determining its future use. Rose et al.'s (2023) discussion of leisure and surveillance makes the politics of observation relevant to proposals for collecting data within everyday leisure.

text.text: An exhibition that invites participation should therefore not assume that measurement is unobtrusive, ethically self-evident, or free of influence on the experience.
These literatures inform a common analytical discipline: separate what the setting makes possible, what people report or produce, and what the researcher infers.
The present evaluation uses several materials to describe complementary dimensions of participation.
It does not assume that their coexistence establishes a common mechanism, or that combining them resolves their individual limitations.
The study was a multi-method, single-arm observational evaluation of Art of Perception and selected surrounding festival activities.
Quantitative surveys and participatory materials were collected during Creative Lab Festival 2026 and considered together at interpretation.
The exhibition ran from March 30 to May 17, 2026, at the Rupa Rahul Bajaj Centre for Environment and Art within Empress Botanical Garden, Pune.
Exhibition admission was free, with attendance estimated at approximately 3,800.
The wider festival included an academic Unconference on March 27-29, experiential workshops, art weekends, a nature weekend, and a children's sensory summer camp.
The primary analytic focus is the exhibition survey.
Workshop drawings provide complementary evidence from another part of the festival, not repeated observations of the same exhibition participants.
Feedback from the academic Unconference is treated only as separate program context in the supplementary material.
This distinction prevents experiences in differently organized activities from being combined into a single estimate of exhibition benefit.
Ethics approval was reported under ARISA Foundation IRB protocol 061123-AF-R²-A2.
Survey participation was voluntary and consented.
The evaluation arose within the organizing institution, and most authors are affiliated with that institution.
This organizational proximity offers knowledge of the setting but also makes favorable interpretation and socially desirable responses relevant concerns.
The findings are therefore presented as an internally situated evaluation rather than an independent impact assessment.
The seven zones offered different modes of engagement (Table 1).
text.formatted: The seven zones offered different modes of engagement (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Zone 1 displayed visitors' heart rate variability through ambient light and sound while inviting paced, exhale-lengthened breathing.
This installation drew on the rationale for breathing-linked biofeedback, but no physiological outcomes are analyzed here (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014).
text.formatted: This installation drew on the rationale for breathing-linked biofeedback, but no physiological outcomes are analyzed here <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Zone 2 coupled movement to projected imagery.
Zone 3 invited interpretation of one artwork through sensory features, affective responses, and personal or cultural meaning, using the labels "The Eye," "The Feeling," and "The Storyteller."
These lenses drew on accounts of interacting systems in aesthetic experience (Chatterjee & Vartanian, 2014).
text.formatted: These lenses drew on accounts of interacting systems in aesthetic experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Chatterjee & Vartanian, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Zone 4 presented visual illusions.
Zone 5 displayed six unfamiliar faces and invited a token beneath the one that appeared friendliest; accumulated votes were visible.
Zone 6 presented work by neurodivergent artists in a quiet, unhurried space without a prescribed route or pace.
Zone 7 directed attention outdoors to the botanical garden.
Figure 1 illustrates selected installations.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> illustrates selected installations.

text.text: The evaluation did not link individual outcomes to time spent in particular zones, so the analyses concern the visit as a whole rather than the effect of any component.
The attendance register contained 3,673 analysable sign-in entries.
These entries describe recorded attendance rather than a verified count of unique visitors.
The survey contained 200 matched participant identifiers: 100 using an early questionnaire and 100 using a revised version introduced during the exhibition.
Of these, 166 had complete responses on all six outcomes at both time points.
Valid paired observations for individual outcomes ranged from 174 to 178.

Additional materials comprised 148 responses to "one thing I know about the brain" and 146 to "one thing I learnt about the brain"; 1,339 tokens in the face-judgment installation; a separate pilot in which 21 raters judged the beauty of the same six face images; and 65 drawings from seven workshops.
The units are consequently different: survey participants, written responses, tokens, pilot raters, and drawings.
They are not pooled into a total sample, and no person-level linkage across these sources is assumed.

Six single-item self-reports addressed bodily relaxation, understanding perception as a brainbody process, trust in perception, skepticism of first impressions, experiencing the world differently, and connection to nature.
The items were written in accessible language for completion in the exhibition.
The full pre-and post-test instruments are reproduced in the supplementary material (Section S5).
Their wording was aligned with exhibition content, rather than drawn from a validated multidimensional measure of leisure experience or well-being.
Consequently, the analysis concerns these reported responses, not a global well-being construct.
Scores were transformed to a 0-100 range, with higher values indicating more of the named outcome.
For scales beginning at 1, the transformation subtracted the minimum possible score, divided by the possible range, and multiplied by 100.
Three outcomes changed from three-point to five-point response scales in the revised questionnaire.
These were rescaled within questionnaire version before pooling.
This transformation provides a common numerical range; it does not establish equivalence between response formats or remove potential differences between the two recruitment periods.
No values were imputed, and each outcome used its available valid pairs.
For each outcome, the analysis estimated pre-and post-visit means, paired mean change, and a bootstrap 95% confidence interval using 20,000 resamples.
Standardized paired mean changes (d) are also reported.
Two-sided sign-flip permutation tests used 100,000 Monte Carlo resamples, with Holm adjustment across six outcomes.
The validity of this inference depends on the relevant exchangeability or symmetry assumptions; bounded, ordinal-origin data do not automatically guarantee them.
Paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were included as sensitivity analyses.
Positive individual score changes are reported descriptively in the supplement.
A positive change is not necessarily clinically or practically important, and increasing trust in perception is not intrinsically a desirable outcome.
Accordingly, the six items are not interpreted as a validated benefit index, and an average across them is not the paper's substantive endpoint.

The written responses were classified using an exploratory, deductive dictionary covering eight content areas: neuroplasticity/change; brain-body-emotion links; perception/illusion/prediction; brain-art-creativity; nature connection; neurodiversity/inclusion; specific neuroanatomy; and metacognition/humility.
Responses could contain more than one code.
This was a rapid computational content analysis, not an inductive thematic analysis or an assessment of conceptual accuracy.
We report frequencies for each prompt descriptively.
The two prompt datasets differ in response totals and are not treated here as a verified matched sample.
Moreover, the prompts elicit different kinds of statements, so their contrast is not interpreted as a paired learning-gain test.
The workshop feedback procedure supplied associations between colors and affective descriptors, and between shapes and experiential domains.
Blue indicated calm/grounded, yellow energized/interested, red intensity/overwhelm, and grey disconnection/uncertainty.
A square represented awareness/clarity, a triangle curiosity, a hexagon emotion, and a circle connection/community.
Drawings were coded using this workshop-specific key.
Counts therefore represent markings interpreted within a prompted response format, not universal meanings of colors or shapes.
The materials lacked independent dual coding, and inter-rater reliability could not be estimated.
As the drawings were collected only after workshops, they describe post-workshop representations rather than measured change.
The separate pilot rated each face's beauty on a five-point scale.
The exhibition vote totals and their percentages were compared descriptively with those ratings.
The analysis also calculated a chi-square test against equal vote shares and a Spearman correlation across the six images; these are retained in the supplement with their limitations.
The 1,339 tokens are not 1,339 independent observations of the beauty-friendliness relationship.
That comparison has six image-level units, while the public vote display, fixed positions, and unknown repeat participation complicate interpretation of the token distribution.
Integration proceeded by identifying what each source could address and where its evidential reach ended.

text.text: Shared subject matter across sources was considered complementarity rather than independent confirmation when populations, timing, or constructs differed.
This approach retains useful contextual material without allowing agreement in broad theme to substitute for measurement of a common process.
The sign-in register recorded 62.1% of entries as female, 37.3% as male, and 0.6% as unknown or other.
These figures characterize the attendance records, not the demographic composition of the matched survey sample.
They indicate recorded participation across age groups but do not establish representativeness, inclusion of particular underserved communities, or equal opportunity to attend.
There were 200 matched survey identifiers, but no individual outcome had complete data for all 200.
The outcome-specific sample sizes in Table 2 are therefore the relevant denominators for the reported changes.

text.text: The 166 complete cases are used only for the supplementary exploratory summaries across items.
Five outcomes increased after Holm correction (Table 2; Figure 2).

text.text: Bodily relaxation changed from 59.4 to 82.3 on the harmonized 0-100 scale, with a paired mean change of 22.9 points, 95% CI [18.1, 27.8], and reported d = 0.69.

The remaining statistically significant increases were smaller: understanding perception as a brain-body process, 11.0 points [4.2, 18.0]; skepticism of first impressions, 5.1 [1.6, 8.6]; experiencing the world differently, 5.7 [2.0, 9.3]; and connection to nature, 6.5 [3.3, 9.8].
Trust in perception increased by 2.4 points, with a confidence interval spanning zero [-1.0, 5.9] and Holm-adjusted p = .196.
The results therefore do not support an increase on every item.

However, the difference between one significant result and one nonsignificant result does not establish that their changes differ statistically, and this pattern does not rule out demand characteristics.
Average change also should not be confused with the number of individuals showing a positive score difference.
Bodily relaxation increased for 103 of 178 respondents (57.9%), whereas understanding perception as a brain-body process increased for 32 of 178 (18.0%).
Several baseline means were already high.
The response formats, initial scores, and distribution of changes therefore matter when interpreting these percentages.
The data do not establish a threshold for a meaningful improvement, nor whether visitors retained any change after leaving.
Specific neuroanatomy was the most frequent code in prior-knowledge responses, appearing in 33 of 148 (22.3%).

Learning responses most often contained brain-art-creativity (44/146, 30.1%), perception/illusion/prediction (38/146, 26.0%), metacognition/humility (37/146, 25.3%), and neuroplasticity/change (36/146, 24.7%).
Nature connection appeared in 13 learning responses (8.9%), and neurodiversity/inclusion in six (4.1%).
Full frequencies are supplied in Supplementary Table S2.

text.text: These distributions identify content visitors chose to mention under the two prompts.
They are consistent with the exhibition's emphasis on perception, artistic experience, and connections across domains.

They do not show that an individual replaced an anatomical understanding with a more sophisticated one, that the statements were scientifically accurate, or that visitors acquired transferable metacognitive skills.
In particular, a dictionary category labeled metacognition/humility is not a direct measure of either capacity.
The six receptacles accumulated between 189 and 261 tokens.
Image 1 received the largest share (19.5%) and Image 3 the smallest (14.1%); those images also occupied the highest and lowest positions in the separate beauty-rating pilot.
The middle ordering did not correspond consistently with beauty ratings.
The image-level rank association was positive but imprecise with only six stimuli (reported ρ = .70, p = .13).
The installation made a collective pattern of judgments visible, which was part of the participatory design.
Its distribution does not establish why visitors chose particular faces.

Although attractiveness-based trait judgments are a relevant background construct (Dion et al., 1972), alternative influences include facial expression, image placement, visible previous choices, and repeat voting.

text.text: Nor can the tokens be linked to the survey's increase in skepticism of first impressions.
The installation provides a context for reflection on judgment, not evidence that it reduced bias.
Connection/community markings appeared in 55 of 65 drawings (84.6%), curiosity in 46 (70.8%), and awareness/clarity in 45 (69.2%).
Calm/grounded and energized/interested markings co-occurred in 45 drawings (69.2%).
Emotion markings appeared in 29 (44.6%), intensity/overwhelm in 18 (27.7%), and disconnection/uncertainty in seven (10.8%).
Supplementary Table S4 provides the complete descriptive coding results and interval estimates.

text.text: These representations included different and sometimes coexisting affective descriptors.

Cooccurrence of calm and energy is not itself evidence of emotional regulation, and red or grey markings cannot be assigned a positive or negative personal meaning beyond the response key without participants' explanations.
The drawings nevertheless indicate that a single overall satisfaction score would not exhaust what this particular feedback format recorded.
Across sources, the clearest evidence of temporal difference is the paired survey.
The texts identify reported learning content, the votes describe aggregate participation, and the drawings characterize prompted post-workshop expression.
Together they broaden the description of the festival, but they do not independently verify a single outcome or demonstrate the complete operation of a well-being framework.
Table 3 makes those distinctions explicit.

text.text: The findings support a bounded but useful account of cultural leisure.
Respondents reported immediate differences in bodily relaxation, selected beliefs and appraisals, and connection to nature after a free arts-science visit.
Those results are compatible with restorative and reflective possibilities occurring within the same setting.
They do not demonstrate that all visitors experienced both, that one produced the other, or that exhibition design caused either.
The contribution is therefore not a general discovery that brief leisure can matter.
It is a case-based way of connecting distinct opportunities for experience with the kinds of evidence needed to evaluate them.
The design-experience-evidence matrix addresses a practical interpretive problem.
A provider may install biofeedback to support relaxation, provide open routes to support autonomy, or invite collective activity to support affiliation.
These are reasonable intentions, but each requires a different evaluation.
In this study, relaxation was directly queried, whereas experienced autonomy and affiliation were not measured in the exhibition survey.
Keeping those distinctions visible enables readers to design a more informative evaluation rather than infer success from the presence of an installation or from a favorable overall response.

This approach complements experience-centered leisure scholarship by treating the visit as heterogeneous and open to interpretation, rather than as a uniform dose of an activity (Stewart, 1998; Packer & Ballantyne, 2016).

text.text: It also brings experience design into a more cautious relationship with well-being frameworks.
Mechanism theories identify questions worth investigating; they do not convert content-aligned single items into measurements of those mechanisms (Newman et al., 2014; Fancourt et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Mechanism theories identify questions worth investigating; they do not convert content-aligned single items into measurements of those mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Newman et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Fancourt et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The transferable outcome is an analytical discipline: specify the opportunity, measure the relevant experience, and reserve claims about mechanism or durability for designs that can support them.
The distinctive feature of this exhibition was the possibility of moving between undergoing an experience and noticing its construction.
A visual illusion can be encountered as a puzzle and as a prompt to question immediate certainty.
A movement-responsive projection can make bodily action noticeable without requiring a prior scientific vocabulary.

Such arrangements connect the pleasurable discovery described in educational leisure with bodily ways of knowing explored in leisure scholarship (Packer, 2006; Bultitude & Sardo, 2012; Borovica, 2020).
text.formatted: Such arrangements connect the pleasurable discovery described in educational leisure with bodily ways of knowing explored in leisure scholarship <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Packer, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bultitude & Sardo, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Borovica, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The survey and written responses provide limited support for examining this relationship further: respondents' self-reported understanding of perception increased, and perception-related content was prominent among learning statements.
They do not show the moment-to-moment process by which an experience became a reflection.
Embodied reflexivity is consequently a useful account of what the installations invited and a proposition for subsequent research, not a new capacity demonstrated in participants.
Observations of interaction, visitors' explanations in their own terms, and later accounts of remembered encounters would address that process more directly.
The case also illustrates why cognitive, restorative, and evaluative outcomes should remain distinguishable.
Greater acknowledgment of perceptual construction need not require global distrust of perception.
Equally, feeling relaxed does not entail becoming more skeptical of social impressions.
The present pattern justifies retaining multiple outcomes; it does not establish a statistical dissociation between them.
This distinction protects the study's substantive interest without overstating what its measurements resolve.
For exhibition and leisure providers, the immediate implication is to consider a repertoire of modes of engagement rather than a single prescribed emotional journey.
Art of Perception combined stimulating displays, opportunities to examine an interpretation, a quiet gallery, and an outdoor setting.
Its findings make relaxation and reflection reasonable priorities for future design tests, while the workshop drawings remind evaluators to allow for intensity and uncertainty.
The case does not identify an optimal sequence or prove that quiet zones caused relaxation.
One testable design proposition is that optional transitions between stimulation and pause may support a wider range of visitor preferences than a uniformly immersive route.
A second is that invitations to reflect after an embodied activity may make scientific content approachable without converting the visit into a lesson.
Neither proposition requires every visitor to complete every activity or produce a learning outcome.
Choice to observe, skip, stop, or simply enjoy an artwork should remain part of the provision rather than be interpreted automatically as failed engagement.
This recommendation follows the distinction between an available opportunity and an experienced benefit; it is not a finding that autonomy increased.

text.text: For example, a provider considering a breathing installation should first distinguish the value of a place to pause from the added value of biofeedback technology.
This evaluation cannot make that comparison, and therefore does not support a claim that the technology is necessary, inexpensive, or cost-effective.
Similarly, the garden is part of the context in which connection to nature increased, not an isolated causal ingredient.
Comparison with a garden-only visit would make the practical question more informative.
The proposed use of the results is thus neither to replicate seven installations as an evidencebased package nor to advertise improved mental health.
It is to use the observed profile to choose a small number of explicit design questions, preserve visitors' freedom to engage differently, and collect measures capable of informing the next decision.

Measures developed for museum wellbeing evaluation offer one starting point for improving outcome coverage, with further adaptation and testing needed for the local languages, ages, and setting (Thomson & Chatterjee, 2015).
text.formatted: Measures developed for museum wellbeing evaluation offer one starting point for improving outcome coverage, with further adaptation and testing needed for the local languages, ages, and setting <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Thomson & Chatterjee, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Free exhibition admission reduced a specified financial requirement.
Nothing in the evaluation establishes which other barriers were removed, who remained absent, or whether all visitors could use the installations on equal terms.
A constraints perspective therefore changes the practical question from whether provision is free to which conditions enable different people to participate (Crawford et al., 1991).
text.formatted: A constraints perspective therefore changes the practical question from whether provision is free to which conditions enable different people to participate <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Crawford et al., 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Future evaluation should examine the reach of recruitment, reasons for nonattendance, access to the site, and experiences of sensory or social discomfort alongside the responses of those who completed a survey.
The neurodivergent artists' gallery also raises questions of representation and authority.
The present audience-focused data cannot establish the artists' experience of inclusion, their control over interpretation, or the professional value of participation.
Disability-arts scholarship makes those questions relevant rather than peripheral (Darcy et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Disability-arts scholarship makes those questions relevant rather than peripheral <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Darcy et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Future design should involve artists and intended visitor communities in deciding how work is presented and how accessibility is assessed, rather than treating representation on a wall as sufficient evidence of inclusion.

The relevance of co-design and adaptable interaction identified by MacRitchie et al. (2023) supports asking these questions without transferring findings from a clinical population to this public audience.
The Indian setting adds contextual specificity, not a representative account of Indian leisure.

We did not collect sufficiently detailed accounts of linguistic, class, caste, disability, or neighborhood differences to explain how the experience was culturally situated. Iwasaki's (2008) emphasis on meaning in global contexts makes this an agenda for deeper inquiry rather than permission to interpret the observed responses through assumed cultural characteristics.

text.text: Contextual extension requires attending to local meanings as well as adding a new geographic location to an existing evidence base.
The exhibition demonstrates how participatory activities can also produce research material.
It does not establish that embedding measurement reduces reactivity or that additional materials automatically produce stronger causal evidence.
Visible votes may influence later votes.
Writing a learning statement may prompt reflection rather than merely record it.
A supplied drawing key structures what can be expressed.
These are features of the research encounter, not inconveniences eliminated by calling the venue a public laboratory.
Arts-based leisure scholarship offers a more demanding methodological direction than collecting more visual feedback alone.
Creative analytic practice and a/r/tography treat representation and inquiry as substantive processes, not decoration around a numerical result (Parry & Johnson, 2007; Schultz & Legg, 2020).
text.formatted: Creative analytic practice and a/r/tography treat representation and inquiry as substantive processes, not decoration around a numerical result <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Parry & Johnson, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Schultz & Legg, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In a future study, participants could interpret their drawings, identify meanings absent from the coding key, or help decide which questions the evaluation should ask.
These would be changes to the research relationship, not procedures claimed to have occurred here.
Accountability also requires distinguishing enjoyment of an installation from consent to research use.
The concerns raised by Rose et al. (2023) suggest explicit attention to visibility, data retention, and the ability to decline measurement without losing access to an activity.

text.text: The present study does not test a privacy or governance model.
Its methodological contribution is the recognition that experience design and evidence production must be examined together, including the possibility that the latter alters the former.
Under those conditions, participatory evaluation can be useful without being described as naturally nonintrusive or inherently emancipatory.
The single-arm pre-post design cannot isolate exhibition effects from expectations, repeated questioning, time, companions, the garden, or other features of a visit.
Self-selection into attendance and survey completion limits generalization.
The absence of a comparison group and delayed follow-up prevents causal and durability claims.
Heterogeneous item changes do not eliminate demand characteristics.
Without participant-level exposure information, the relative contribution of the seven zones remains unknown.
Measurement is a second limitation.
The six accessible items offer restricted construct coverage, and several had high baseline scores.
The mid-run change in response formats complicates pooling even after rescaling.
Stable wording, common response options, version-specific estimates, and sensitivity checks for the assumptions underlying the reported tests are needed before stronger comparative claims.
The standardized effect-size denominator should be specified in the reproducible analysis, and none of the reported d values should be read as a treatment effect.
There is no validated clinical or practical threshold for these item changes.
The additional sources have different limits.
Dictionary coding does not establish learning quality; unverified person-level matching and different prompts preclude a paired learning-gain claim.
The face installation has only six stimuli and uncontrolled social and positional influences.
Drawings were post-only, prompted, and not independently dual-coded; they were not linked to exhibition survey outcomes.
These strands therefore broaden description but cannot repair the causal or psychometric weaknesses of the survey.
Organizational proximity further warrants transparency about who recruited, facilitated, coded, and interpreted the material.
A useful next study would prioritize a few comparisons rather than add more loosely related outcomes.
It could compare an exhibition visit with a garden-only or other cultural visit, using consistent measures and recording exposure and immediate experience.
Within the exhibition, ethically designed comparisons could examine a quiet pause with and without technological feedback, or alternative orders of activity and explanation.
A delayed assessment could then ask what was remembered, reused, or discussed with others, distinguishing immediate appraisal from sustained significance.
Finally, participant-led interpretation and targeted access research could address whose experiences and meanings are missing.
These proposals follow from the present uncertainties; they are not evidence that any specific design feature has already been validated.
Art of Perception linked bodily activity, scientific explanation, artistic encounter, and opportunities for pause within a free cultural leisure setting.
Its evaluation recorded immediate self-reported changes, most prominently in bodily relaxation, alongside varied written and visual responses.
The study's value lies less in a general claim that leisure is beneficial than in showing how an exhibition's different opportunities can be connected to specific, limited forms of evidence.

The design-experience-evidence distinction gives leisure researchers and providers a practical way to use the case: identify the experience a feature is intended to support, examine what visitors actually report or do, and specify the comparison needed before claiming a mechanism or enduring benefit.

This approach accommodates reflection and relaxation without making either compulsory, values participation without equating it with inclusion, and retains the possibility of meaningful cultural leisure without treating every favorable response as proof of transformation.
